P1.bio: Mr. Utterson is a lawyer of Gaunt Street, kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and old friend of Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past, troubled by old sins. Utterson kept watch by the by-street door until he accosted Hyde, studied his face, and was deeply disturbed. He then learned from Poole that Jekyll was out and that Hyde had a key. He now fears Jekyll is in deep waters.

He now remains Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor, unaware of Hyde's identity.

P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, connoisseur, and friend of Mr. Utterson and Dr. Lanyon. After dinner with Utterson, Jekyll refused to hear more of Hyde, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hyde for his sake. He is now painfully situated, his position strange and not mended by talking.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

He then identified Sir Danvers Carew's body and searched Hyde's rooms. He is now obsessed with finding and seeing Hyde.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

He then identified Sir Danvers Carew's body and searched Hyde's rooms. He is now obsessed with finding and seeing Hyde.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, connoisseur, and friend of Mr. Utterson and Dr. Lanyon. He is large, well-made, smooth-faced, with a slyish cast, showing capacity and kindness and warm affection for Utterson. Over ten years ago Lanyon found him too fanciful and wrong in mind. His will leaves all his possessions to Edward Hyde, who inherits if Jekyll vanishes. After dinner with Utterson, Jekyll refused to hear more of Hyde, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hyde for his sake. He is now painfully situated, his position strange and not mended by talking.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: G. J. Utterson is a lawyer, a kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and an old friend of both Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past who is troubled by old sins. After Enfield told him of a faceless figure at a by-street door, he lay awake haunted, kept watch by that door, and resolved to hunt for Hyde. He accosted Hyde, studied his face, and was deeply disturbed. He raised Jekyll's will, promised to bear with Hyde, identified Sir Danvers Carew's body, recognized his own stick as the weapon, searched Hyde's rooms, and heard Guest find Hyde's letter identical with Jekyll's hand. He dined with Jekyll and Lanyon, then found Jekyll shut against him and Lanyon refusing Jekyll's name. After Lanyon's funeral he opened the sealed envelope, whose enclosure must wait for Jekyll's death or disappearance. He now prefers speaking with Poole at the door rather than entering.

P3.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. P7.name: Dr. Jekyll

P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a doctor, connoisseur and old friend of Utterson and Lanyon, known for charities and religion. He is fifty, large, well-made and smooth-faced, with a slyish cast. Over ten years ago Lanyon found him too fanciful and wrong in mind. His will leaves all his possessions to Edward Hyde, who inherits if Jekyll vanishes. When Utterson raised the will and Hyde, Jekyll paled, refused to hear more, called Lanyon a hide-bound pedant, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hyde for his sake. He swore he would never set eyes on Hyde again, gave Utterson Hyde's letter to judge, admitted Hyde dictated the will, then emerged and resumed old friendships. He later shut his door against Utterson, wrote of an incurable quarrel, vowed extreme seclusion and an unnameable punishment. He now confines himself over the laboratory and is silent.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: G. J. Utterson is a lawyer, a kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and an old friend of both Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past who is troubled by old sins. After Enfield told him of a faceless figure at a by-street door, he lay awake haunted, kept watch by that door, and resolved to hunt for Hyde. He accosted Hyde, studied his face, and was deeply disturbed. He raised Jekyll's will, promised to bear with Hyde, identified Sir Danvers Carew's body, recognized his own stick as the weapon, searched Hyde's rooms, and heard Guest find Hyde's letter identical with Jekyll's hand. He dined with Jekyll and Lanyon, then found Jekyll shut against him and Lanyon refusing Jekyll's name. After Lanyon's funeral he opened the sealed envelope, whose enclosure must wait for Jekyll's death or disappearance. He now prefers speaking with Poole at the door rather than entering.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Mr. Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town. He dislikes asking questions and calls it delicacy. On a Sunday walk with Utterson, he pointed his cane at a sinister door and said it was connected with a very odd story. He collared a man who had trampled a girl, forced him to pay a hundred pounds, and spent the night with him in his chambers before taking him to the bank, where the cheque proved genuine. He called the door place Black Mail House, described the door house, named the man as Hyde, and confirmed Hyde still has the key and used it a week ago. He agreed with Utterson never to refer to the matter again.

P3.name: the man in the middle
P3.tagline: Tramples a girl, pays with a cheque
P3.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description, and disappeared into the house. The maid saw him beat Sir Danvers Carew to death with a cane. He had few familiars, no traceable family, no photograph, and several thousand pounds to his credit. He has vanished from police knowledge; rewards are offered.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a doctor, connoisseur and old friend of Utterson and Lanyon, known for charities and religion. He is fifty, large, well-made and smooth-faced, with a slyish cast. Over ten years ago Lanyon found him too fanciful and wrong in mind. His will leaves all his possessions to Edward Hyde, who inherits if Jekyll vanishes. When Utterson raised the will and Hyde, Jekyll paled, refused to hear more, called Lanyon a hide-bound pedant, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hyde for his sake. He swore he would never set eyes on Hyde again, gave Utterson Hyde's letter to judge, admitted Hyde dictated the will, then emerged and resumed old friendships. He later shut his door against Utterson, wrote of an incurable quarrel, vowed extreme seclusion and an unnameable punishment. He now confines himself over the laboratory and is silent.

P8.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old friend of Utterson and formerly of Dr. Jekyll. He is boisterous, decided and theatrical but genuine. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind. When Utterson asked about Hyde, Lanyon had never heard of him. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened the sealed envelope Lanyon left, whose enclosure is not to be opened till Jekyll's death or disappearance. recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: G. J. Utterson is a lawyer, a kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and an old friend of both Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past who is troubled by old sins. After Enfield told him of a faceless figure at a by-street door, he lay awake haunted, kept watch by that door, and resolved to hunt for Hyde. He accosted Hyde, studied his face, and was deeply disturbed. He raised Jekyll's will, promised to bear with Hyde, identified Sir Danvers Carew's body, recognized his own stick as the weapon, searched Hyde's rooms, and heard Guest find Hyde's letter identical with Jekyll's hand. He dined with Jekyll and Lanyon, then found Jekyll shut against him and Lanyon refusing Jekyll's name. After Lanyon's funeral he opened the sealed envelope, whose enclosure must wait for Jekyll's death or disappearance. He now prefers speaking with Poole at the door rather than entering.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Mr. Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town. He dislikes asking questions and calls it delicacy. On a Sunday walk with Utterson, he pointed his cane at a sinister door and said it was connected with a very odd story. He collared a man who had trampled a girl, forced him to pay a hundred pounds, and spent the night with him in his chambers before taking him to the bank, where the cheque proved genuine. He called the door place Black Mail House, described the door house, named the man as Hyde, and confirmed Hyde still has the key and used it a week ago. He agreed with Utterson never to refer to the matter again.

P3.name: the man in the middle
P3.tagline: Tramples a girl, pays with a cheque
P3.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description, and disappeared into the house. The maid saw him beat Sir Danvers Carew to death with a cane. He had few familiars, no traceable family, no photograph, and several thousand pounds to his credit. He has vanished from police knowledge; rewards are offered.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a doctor, connoisseur and old friend of Utterson and Lanyon, known for charities and religion. He is fifty, large, well-made and smooth-faced, with a slyish cast. Over ten years ago Lanyon found him too fanciful and wrong in mind. His will leaves all his possessions to Edward Hyde, who inherits if Jekyll vanishes. When Utterson raised the will and Hyde, Jekyll paled, refused to hear more, called Lanyon a hide-bound pedant, said he could be rid of Hyde whenever he chose, and asked Utterson to help Hyde for his sake. He swore he would never set eyes on Hyde again, gave Utterson Hyde's letter to judge, admitted Hyde dictated the will, then emerged and resumed old friendships. He later shut his door against Utterson, wrote of an incurable quarrel, vowed extreme seclusion and an unnameable punishment. He now confines himself over the laboratory and is silent.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P3.name: the man in the middle
P3.tagline: Tramples a girl, pays with a cheque
P3.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description, and disappeared into the house. The maid saw him beat Sir Danvers Carew to death with a cane. He had few familiars, no traceable family, no photograph, and several thousand pounds to his credit. He has vanished from police knowledge; rewards are offered.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
P7.bio: Dr. Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, owner of the house with laboratory and cabinet, and the friend and client of Mr. Utterson. He is tall and well built, known for charities and religion, but has become fanciful and estranged from Dr. Lanyon. His will left all his possessions to Edward Hyde, and he admitted Hyde dictated its terms. He swore he would never set eyes on Hyde again, then resumed his old friendships before shutting his door against Utterson and vowing extreme seclusion. He was last seen sitting sadly at the middle window, declining to walk out. He is said to have been made away with eight days ago, and his body has not been found.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor
P8.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old friend of Utterson and formerly of Dr. Jekyll. He is boisterous, decided and theatrical but genuine. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind. When Utterson asked about Hyde, Lanyon had never heard of him. He dined with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, but later Utterson found him visibly decayed; Lanyon declared himself a doomed man who would never recover, refused to hear Jekyll's name and called him dead to him. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened the sealed envelope Lanyon left, whose enclosure is not to be opened till Jekyll's death or disappearance. He is dead.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P3.bio: Edward Hyde is a young man in whom Dr. Jekyll takes great interest, the favourite of Jekyll, and the heir named in Jekyll's will. He is merciless, inspires enduring hatred, and impresses beholders with a sense of unexpressed deformity. He trampled over a girl's body and left her screaming, was forced by threats of scandal to pay a hundred pounds, and led Enfield's group to a door where he returned with gold and a cheque. He later met Utterson at that door, gave his address in Soho, angrily accused Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description, and disappeared into the house. The maid saw him beat Sir Danvers Carew to death with a cane. He had few familiars, no traceable family, no photograph, and several thousand pounds to his credit. He has vanished from police knowledge; rewards are offered.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir
P7.bio: Dr. Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, owner of the house with laboratory and cabinet, and the friend and client of Mr. Utterson. He is tall and well built, known for charities and religion, but has become fanciful and estranged from Dr. Lanyon. His will left all his possessions to Edward Hyde, and he admitted Hyde dictated its terms. He swore he would never set eyes on Hyde again, then resumed his old friendships before shutting his door against Utterson and vowing extreme seclusion. He was last seen sitting sadly at the middle window, declining to walk out. He is said to have been made away with eight days ago, and his body has not been found.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor
P8.bio: Dr. Lanyon is a doctor with a house in Cavendish Square, an old friend of Utterson and formerly of Dr. Jekyll. He is boisterous, decided and theatrical but genuine. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind. When Utterson asked about Hyde, Lanyon had never heard of him. He dined with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, but later Utterson found him visibly decayed; Lanyon declared himself a doomed man who would never recover, refused to hear Jekyll's name and called him dead to him. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened the sealed envelope Lanyon left, whose enclosure is not to be opened till Jekyll's death or disappearance. He is dead.

P10.name: Poole
P10.tagline: Elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house
P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler of Dr. Jekyll's house and the servant who directs the search after the cabinet is broken open. He is frightened and worn, with a white face and a harsh broken voice, and for about a week he has been unable to bear the situation. He long served Jekyll, admitted Utterson to the cabinet, and reported that Jekyll confined himself over the laboratory. When he came to Utterson's house at night, he said the doctor had shut himself in and he feared foul play. He led Utterson to the laboratory, told of the masked figure, and struck the door with an axe. He now hands Utterson the sealed packet and awaits the police.

P20.name: the voice
P20.tagline: Voice inside the cabinet refusing entry
P20.bio: The voice is the unseen speaker inside Dr. Jekyll's cabinet, heard by Poole and Mr. Utterson during the night search. It complains that it cannot see anyone and begs Utterson for mercy. It is connected to Poole only as the servant who knocks and calls through the door. After Poole reports that the doctor has shut himself in, the voice answers from within and refuses entry. Utterson recognizes it as Hyde's voice and orders the door down. The voice is now silent, its speaker found dead inside the cabinet.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir.
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor.
P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind, and later refused to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him. After dining with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, he was shocked by his own decayed appearance and declared himself a doomed man who would never recover. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened his sealed envelope.

P10.name: Poole
P10.tagline: Elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house.
P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He is afraid and cannot bear it, with a white face and harsh broken voice. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, that Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, and that all servants had orders to obey Hyde. Later he reported Jekyll confined and silent, came to Utterson at night, and said he thought there had been foul play. He and Utterson broke in and found Hyde's body. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

P20.name: the voice
P20.tagline: Voice inside the cabinet refusing entry
P20.bio: The voice is the unseen speaker inside Dr. Jekyll's cabinet, heard by Poole and Mr. Utterson during the night search. It complains that it cannot see anyone and begs Utterson for mercy. It is connected to Poole only as the servant who knocks and calls through the door. After Poole reports that the doctor has shut himself in, the voice answers from within and refuses entry. Utterson recognizes it as Hyde's voice and orders the door down. The voice is now silent, its speaker found dead inside the cabinet.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir.
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor.
P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind, and later refused to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him. After dining with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, he was shocked by his own decayed appearance and declared himself a doomed man who would never recover. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened his sealed envelope.

P10.name: Poole
P10.tagline: Elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house.
P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He is afraid and cannot bear it, with a white face and harsh broken voice. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, that Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, and that all servants had orders to obey Hyde. Later he reported Jekyll confined and silent, came to Utterson at night, and said he thought there had been foul play. He and Utterson broke in and found Hyde's body. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

P20.bio: The voice is the unseen speaker inside Dr. Jekyll's cabinet, heard by Poole and Mr. Utterson during the night search. It complains that it cannot see anyone and begs Utterson for mercy. recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor.
P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind, and later refused to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him. After dining with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, he was shocked by his own decayed appearance and declared himself a doomed man who would never recover. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened his sealed envelope.

P10.tagline: Elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house.
P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He is afraid and cannot bear it, with a white face and harsh broken voice. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, that Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, and that all servants had orders to obey Hyde. Later he reported Jekyll confined and silent, came to Utterson at night, and said he thought there had been foul play. He and Utterson broke in and found Hyde's body. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir.
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.name: Dr. Lanyon
P8.tagline: Utterson's old friend and fellow doctor.
P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind, and later refused to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him. After dining with Jekyll and Utterson as inseparable friends, he was shocked by his own decayed appearance and declared himself a doomed man who would never recover. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened his sealed envelope.

P10.name: Poole
P10.tagline: Elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house.
P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He is afraid and cannot bear it, with a white face and harsh broken voice. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, that Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, and that all servants had orders to obey Hyde. Later he reported Jekyll confined and silent, came to Utterson at night, and said he thought there had been foul play. He and Utterson broke in and found Hyde's body. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir.
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

P22.bio: The small man is a secret midnight visitor who comes in Dr. Jekyll's name to Dr. Lanyon's house. He is small, with a shocking facial expression. At midnight he knocked gently and crouched against the portico pillars; when Lanyon asked if he came from Dr. Jekyll, he gestured yes. He glanced back at a policeman and hurried inside. Lanyon then saw him clearly for the first time and was struck by his appearance. He is currently at Lanyon's house, having come secretly at midnight in Jekyll's name.
