events.text: Utterson and Enfield take their Sunday walk down a by-street.
Enfield points his cane at a sinister door and asks Utterson if he ever remarked it.
Enfield says the door is connected with a very odd story.
Enfield collars the man and brings him back to the group around the child.
The man tramples over the girl's body and leaves her screaming.
The doctor turns sick and white with desire to kill the prisoner.
They threaten scandal and force the man to pay a hundred pounds.
The man leads them to the door, unlocks it, and returns with gold and a cheque.
The man offers to stay until the banks open and cash the cheque himself.
They spend the night in Enfield's chambers and go to the bank next day.
Enfield presents the cheque believing it a forgery, but it proves genuine.
Enfield calls the door place Black Mail House and muses.
Utterson asks if the cheque drawer lives there.
Enfield says he noticed the drawer's address in some square.
Enfield explains his rule of not asking questions.
Enfield describes the door house: no other door, clean shut windows, smoking chimney.
Utterson asks the name of the man who walked over the child.
Enfield names the man as Hyde.
Enfield describes Hyde as deformed and detestable.
Utterson asks if Hyde used a key.
Utterson says he already knows the other party's name.
Enfield confirms Hyde still has the key and used it a week ago.
Enfield and Utterson agree never to refer to the matter again.
Utterson comes home in low spirits and studies Jekyll's will in his business room.
The will leaves all Jekyll's possessions to Edward Hyde, and Hyde inherits if Jekyll vanishes.
Utterson calls the will madness and now fears it is disgrace.
Utterson goes to Cavendish Square to consult his friend Dr. Lanyon.
Lanyon welcomes Utterson warmly as an old school and college friend.
Utterson asks whether he and Lanyon are Jekyll's two oldest friends.
Lanyon says Jekyll became too fanciful and wrong in mind over ten years ago.
Utterson asks Lanyon about Hyde, and Lanyon has never heard of him.
Utterson lies awake all night, haunted by Enfield's tale and the faceless figure.
Utterson keeps watch by the by-street door at all hours until his patience is rewarded.
Utterson resolves to hunt for Hyde, thinking 'If he be Mr. Hyde, I shall be Mr. Seek.'
A small plainly dressed man approaches the door with a key, and Utterson accosts him as Mr. Hyde.
Utterson accosts Hyde and asks to be admitted to see Jekyll.
Hyde tells Utterson that Dr. Jekyll is from home.
Utterson asks to see Hyde's face and studies it.
Hyde gives Utterson his address in Soho.
Hyde angrily accuses Utterson of lying about Jekyll's description.
Hyde snarls, unlocks the door, and disappears into the house.
Utterson walks away deeply disturbed by Hyde's appearance.
Utterson arrives at Jekyll's house and is admitted by Poole.
Poole tells Utterson that Dr. Jekyll has gone out.
Poole confirms Hyde has a key and comes by the dissecting room door.
Poole says all servants have orders to obey Hyde.
Poole says Hyde never dines there and mostly uses the laboratory.
Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.
Utterson stays behind after Jekyll's dinner to speak with him.
Utterson raises the subject of Jekyll's will.
Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant and says he was disappointed in him.
Utterson says he has learned something of young Hyde.
Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more about Hyde.
Utterson offers to help Jekyll out of the matter in confidence.
Jekyll says he can be rid of Mr. Hyde whenever he chooses.
Jekyll says he takes a great interest in poor Hyde.
Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone.
Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights for him.
The maid sees Hyde beat an aged beautiful gentleman with white hair to death with a cane.
The maid faints at the horror of the murder.
The maid wakes at two and calls the police.
The victim's body is found mangled in the lane.
A sealed envelope addressed to Utterson is found on the victim.
Utterson identifies the body as Sir Danvers Carew.
The officer narrates the maid's account and shows the broken stick.
Utterson recognizes the stick as one he gave Henry Jekyll.
Utterson offers to take the officer to Hyde's house.
The old woman lets Utterson and the inspector search Hyde's rooms.
They find the other half of the stick and a burnt cheque book.
The inspector finds several thousand pounds to Hyde's credit at the bank.
The inspector plans to wait for Hyde at the bank and issue handbills.
Mr. Hyde had few familiars and was hard to trace.
The maid's master had seen Hyde only twice.
Hyde's family could not be traced anywhere.
Hyde had never been photographed.
Those who could describe Hyde differed widely.
Observers agreed only on a sense of unexpressed deformity in Hyde.
Utterson is admitted by Poole and received into Jekyll's cabinet.
Utterson asks Jekyll whether he has heard the news.
Jekyll swears he will never set eyes on Hyde again.
Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde to judge.
Jekyll says he burned the envelope and it bore no postmark.
Jekyll admits Hyde dictated the terms of his will.
Poole tells Utterson no letter came except by post.
Utterson hears newsboys crying the murder of an M.P.
Utterson shows Guest the murderer's autograph letter.
Guest compares the letter with Jekyll's note and finds them identical.
Utterson locks the note in his safe and suspects Jekyll of forgery.
Hyde vanishes after Sir Danvers's murder; rewards are offered.
Jekyll emerges from seclusion and resumes his old friendships.
Utterson dines with Jekyll and Lanyon as inseparable friends.
Jekyll shuts his door against Utterson, Poole reporting he is confined.
Utterson visits Lanyon and is shocked by his decayed appearance.
Lanyon declares himself a doomed man who will never recover.
Lanyon refuses to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him.
Utterson writes to Jekyll, who replies of an incurable quarrel.
Jekyll vows extreme seclusion and speaks of an unnameable punishment.
Lanyon takes to his bed and dies within a fortnight.
After the funeral Utterson opens Lanyon's sealed envelope.
The enclosure is not to be opened till Jekyll's death or disappearance.
Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door rather than entering.
Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory and is silent.
Utterson and Enfield stop before the by-street door on their Sunday walk.
Enfield says the Hyde story is at an end and they will never see Hyde again.
Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and shared Enfield's repulsion.
Enfield reveals he learned the door was a back way to Dr. Jekyll's.
They enter the court to look at the windows, Utterson uneasy about Jekyll.
Utterson sees Dr. Jekyll sitting sadly at the middle window.
Utterson greets Jekyll and hopes he is better.
Jekyll replies he is very low and says it will not last long.
Utterson introduces his cousin Mr. Enfield to Dr. Jekyll and invites Jekyll out.
Jekyll declines the walk, saying it is quite impossible and he dare not.
Utterson proposes they stay below and talk from where they are.
Jekyll's smile turns to abject terror and the window is thrust down.
The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror.
Utterson says 'God forgive us' twice.
Poole comes to Utterson's house at night and says something is wrong.
Poole says the doctor has shut himself in the cabinet and he is afraid.
Poole says he thinks there has been foul play.
Utterson rises, takes hat and greatcoat, and follows Poole.
They walk through the cold deserted London streets to the house.
They enter the hall where all the servants are huddled in fear.
The housemaid whimpers and the maid weeps loudly.
Poole orders the knife-boy to bring a candle.
Poole leads Utterson to the laboratory and tells him to listen quietly.
Poole knocks and calls that Utterson asks to see him.
The voice inside complains that it cannot see anyone.
Poole asks whether that was his master's voice; Utterson says it seems much changed.
Poole declares his master was made away with eight days ago.
Utterson calls the tale wild and argues a murderer would not stay.
Poole tells of a week of notes demanding a pure drug from chemists.
Poole hands Utterson a crumpled note from Dr. Jekyll to Messrs. Maw.
Utterson notes the handwriting is the doctor's; Poole says he has seen him.
Poole tells Utterson he saw a masked figure in the cabinet.
Utterson suggests Jekyll suffers a deforming disease and hides his face.
Poole insists the masked thing was not Jekyll but a dwarf.
Utterson resolves to break in the cabinet door.
Poole and Utterson agree to break in together.
Poole fetches an axe and suggests Utterson take the kitchen poker.
Utterson warns Poole they are placing themselves in peril.
Poole says the masked figure was Mr. Hyde.
Utterson says he once spoke with Hyde.
Poole describes Hyde as giving a cold, thin feeling.
Utterson summons Bradshaw and orders him to guard the laboratory door.
Poole and Utterson wait in the theatre and hear pacing footsteps.
Poole says the walker weeps like a woman or lost soul.
Utterson demands to see Jekyll and threatens brute force.
The voice begs Utterson for mercy.
Utterson recognizes the voice as Hyde's and orders the door down.
Poole strikes the door five times with the axe until it bursts.
They peer in and find the contorted body of Edward Hyde.
Utterson concludes Hyde is a self-destroyer by the crushed phial.
Utterson says they must now find Jekyll's body.
Utterson and Poole search the theatre, cabinet, closets and cellar for Jekyll.
They find the by-street door locked with a rusty broken key lying nearby.
They examine the cabinet and find chemical apparatus and white salt on saucers.
They find a pious book annotated by Jekyll with startling blasphemies.
They look into the cheval-glass and see only the room and their own pale faces.
Utterson opens an envelope addressed to him and finds a will naming himself instead of Hyde.
Utterson reads Jekyll's dated note and concludes Jekyll was alive that day and may have fled.
Poole hands Utterson a sealed packet, the third enclosure.
Utterson decides to go home, read the documents, and return before midnight to send for the police.
Lanyon receives a registered letter from Henry Jekyll on the ninth of January.
Jekyll begs Lanyon to help him, saying his life and reason are at stake.
Jekyll orders Poole to wait with a locksmith for Lanyon's arrival.
Jekyll instructs Lanyon to force open his cabinet and take the fourth drawer.
Jekyll asks Lanyon to receive a midnight messenger and hand over the drawer.
Jekyll warns that if the night passes without event, Lanyon has seen the last of him.
Lanyon suspects Jekyll is insane but feels bound to obey the appeal.
Lanyon drives to Jekyll's house, where the butler awaits him.
The carpenter and locksmith work two hours to open Jekyll's cabinet door.
Lanyon takes the drawer, has it packed in straw and a sheet, and returns home.
Lanyon examines the drawer's powders, phial, and book of dated experiments.
Lanyon dismisses his servants and loads an old revolver for self-defence.
At midnight a small man knocks gently and crouches against the portico pillars.
Lanyon asks if the visitor comes from Dr. Jekyll, and the man gestures yes.
The visitor glances back at a policeman and hurries inside.
Lanyon sees the visitor clearly for the first time and is struck by his appearance.
Hyde enters Lanyon's house and urgently asks if he has it
Lanyon rebukes Hyde for forgetting they are unacquainted
Hyde says he comes at the instance of Dr. Henry Jekyll
Lanyon points Hyde to the drawer holding the package
Hyde uncovers the contents and sobs with immense relief
Hyde mixes the red tincture and powder into a changing compound
Hyde offers Lanyon knowledge and power or to leave unwiser
Lanyon agrees to see the end of the inexplicable service
Hyde drinks the glass at one gulp and cries out
Hyde transforms and Henry Jekyll stands before Lanyon
Jekyll confesses his moral turpitude to Lanyon with tears
Lanyon learns the visitor was Hyde, murderer of Carew
Jekyll recounts being born to a large fortune and excellent parts.
He conceals his pleasures and commits to a profound duplicity of life.
He concludes man is not truly one but truly two.
He daydreams of separating his good and evil elements into separate identities.
A side light from the laboratory table reveals the transience of the body.
He compounds a drug to dethrone his powers and substitute a second form.
He hesitates long, knowing he risks death, before testing the theory.
He buys a large quantity of a particular salt from wholesale chemists.
Late one accursed night he compounds the elements and drinks the potion.
Racking pangs and deadly nausea succeed before the agonies subside.
He feels younger, lighter, happier, and conscious of heady recklessness.
He realizes he has lost in stature.
He ventures in his new shape through the house toward his bedroom.
He sees for the first time the appearance of Edward Hyde.
Jekyll theorizes Hyde is smaller and younger because his evil side was less exercised.
Jekyll looks at Hyde in the glass and feels welcome rather than repugnance.
Jekyll drinks the cup again and returns to the body of Henry Jekyll.
Jekyll concludes the projected being was Edward Hyde, wholly evil.
Jekyll furnishes a house in Soho where Hyde is later tracked by police.
Jekyll hires a silent, unscrupulous housekeeper for the Soho house.
Jekyll tells his servants that Mr. Hyde may freely use his square house.
Jekyll draws up the will allowing Hyde to inherit without pecuniary loss.
Jekyll describes Hyde's pleasures turning monstrous and his own vicarious depravity.
Hyde's cruelty to a child angered a passer-by, the doctor, and the child's family.
Hyde pacified them by paying a cheque drawn in Henry Jekyll's name.
Jekyll opened a bank account in Hyde's name and forged a signature for him.
Jekyll woke in his square-house bed but saw his hand was Hyde's.
Jekyll wakes in bed and finds he has become Edward Hyde.
Dressed as Hyde, Jekyll passes through the house and Bradshaw stares and draws back.
Ten minutes later Dr. Jekyll returns to his own shape and feigns breakfast.
Jekyll reflects seriously on the issues and possibilities of his double existence.
Jekyll fears the balance of his nature may be permanently overthrown.
Jekyll notes the drug's power has not always been equally displayed and once failed.
Jekyll realizes he is slowly losing hold of his original and better self.
Jekyll feels he must choose between his two natures.
Jekyll chooses the better part but lacks strength to keep to it.
Jekyll prefers the elderly doctor and bids farewell to Hyde's pleasures.
Jekyll keeps the Soho house and Hyde's clothes as an unconscious reservation.
After two months of severity, Jekyll again swallows the transforming draught.
Jekyll is punished by Hyde's moral insensibility and readiness to evil.
Jekyll listens with impatience to the civilities of his unhappy victim.
Jekyll mauls the unresisting body with delight from every blow.
Jekyll flees the scene, destroys his papers in Soho, and walks the lamplit streets.
Hyde drinks the draught and pledges the dead man.
Henry Jekyll falls on his knees with tears of gratitude and remorse.
Jekyll resolves that Hyde is thenceforth impossible and locks the door.
Jekyll learns Hyde's guilt is known and resolves to redeem the past.
Jekyll labours to relieve suffering and lives quietly for months.
Jekyll, sitting in Regent's Park, suddenly transforms into Hyde.
Hyde realizes he must reach his drugs and thinks of Lanyon.
Hyde takes a hansom to a hotel in Portland Street.
Hyde nearly drags the laughing driver from his perch.
Hyde writes and registers letters to Lanyon and Poole.
Hyde spends the day and night in fear, then walks the streets.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.

P1.name: Mr. Utterson
P1.tagline: Lawyer, kinsman and friend of Enfield
P1.bio: Gabriel John Utterson is a lawyer, the distant kinsman of Richard Enfield, and the friend and legal adviser of Dr. Jekyll. He is a man of steady habits, uneasy and concerned for Jekyll, and known as the last good influence on downgoing men. He introduced Enfield to Jekyll and long handled Jekyll's affairs, including a will naming Hyde as heir. When Poole came to him at night fearing foul play, Utterson followed him to Jekyll's house, questioned the servants, and resolved to break in. After the cabinet door was burst open, he found Hyde's body and searched for Jekyll. He now holds Jekyll's sealed packet and intends to read the documents and return before midnight to send for the police.

P2.name: Mr. Richard Enfield
P2.tagline: Utterson's distant kinsman, man about town
P2.bio: Richard Enfield is Utterson's distant kinsman and a man about town, acquainted with Dr. Jekyll. He dislikes asking questions and calls this delicacy. He once collared a man who walked over a child and forced him to pay a hundred pounds, then spent the night in his chambers and proved the cheque genuine at the bank. He named the man as Hyde and described him as deformed and detestable. He later learned the sinister door was a back way to Jekyll's house. On a Sunday walk with Utterson he said the Hyde story was at an end, and after seeing Jekyll at the window he left the court in silence, pale with horror.

P7.name: Dr. Jekyll
P7.tagline: Doctor whose will names Hyde as heir.
P7.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment. On the ninth of January he begged Lanyon to force open his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and receive a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeyed, and Jekyll confessed his moral turpitude with tears.

P8.bio: Hastie Lanyon is a doctor and colleague of Henry Jekyll, and an old friend of Mr. Utterson. He is cautious and suspicious of Jekyll's sanity. Over ten years ago he judged Jekyll too fanciful and wrong in mind, and later refused to hear Jekyll's name, calling him dead to him. He took to his bed and died within a fortnight. After his funeral Utterson opened his sealed envelope.

P10.bio: Poole is the elderly butler at Dr. Jekyll's house, obeyed by the housemaid, cook, and knife-boy, and directed by Mr. Utterson in the search. He is afraid and cannot bear it, with a white face and harsh broken voice. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, that Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, and that all servants had orders to obey Hyde. Later he reported Jekyll confined and silent, came to Utterson at night, and said he thought there had been foul play. He and Utterson broke in and found Hyde's body. He currently awaits Lanyon's arrival with a locksmith.

recaps.text: During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls a story: a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque. The cheque proved genuine. Enfield names the man Hyde, deformed and detestable, who still holds the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death and fainted. At two she called police; the mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Utterson asks if Jekyll has heard the news; Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Hearing newsboys cry an M.P.’s murder, Utterson shows Guest the murderer’s letter. Guest finds it identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After Sir Danvers Carew’s murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, dining with Utterson and Lanyon. Then Jekyll shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. Jekyll writes of an incurable quarrel and extreme seclusion. Lanyon dies within a fortnight. After the funeral, Utterson opens Lanyon’s sealed envelope, not to be opened till Jekyll’s death or disappearance. Utterson prefers speaking with Poole at the door; Poole reports Jekyll confines himself over the laboratory, silent.

On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at the by-street door. Enfield says the Hyde affair is over, but Utterson admits he once saw Hyde and felt the same repulsion. Enfield reveals the door is Dr. Jekyll's back way. Looking up, Utterson sees Jekyll sadly at the middle window. Jekyll says he is very low and it will not last long. He declines their walk, saying he dare not. When Utterson suggests talking from below, Jekyll's smile becomes abject terror and the window is thrust down. The two men leave the court in silence, pale with horror, Utterson saying “God forgive us” twice.

Poole comes to Utterson at night, fearing foul play. They walk to Jekyll’s house, where servants huddle terrified. Poole leads Utterson to the cabinet; a changed voice refuses them. Poole claims Jekyll was murdered eight days ago and saw a masked dwarf—Mr. Hyde. Utterson resolves to break in. Poole strikes the door five times with an axe. Inside lies Hyde’s contorted body, a crushed phial nearby. They search for Jekyll but find only chemicals, a blasphemous book, a will naming Utterson, and a sealed packet. Utterson plans to read the documents and return before midnight.

Dr. Lanyon receives a desperate letter from Henry Jekyll, who begs him to break into his cabinet, take the fourth drawer, and hand it to a midnight messenger. Lanyon obeys, waits armed, and admits a small, crouching man who claims to come from Jekyll. The visitor mixes and drinks the drawer's chemicals, then transforms before Lanyon's eyes into Henry Jekyll, who tearfully confesses that the messenger was Hyde, murderer of Sir Danvers Carew.
